title: Day 55 · Week 7, Day 6 — Myths: lifting causes miscarriage, arms over her head wrap the cord round the neck, and she's eating for two
summary: The fourth Myths episode, closing Week 7. Your baby is 10–14.5 mm at Carnegie stage 17, ~41 days post-fertilization: definite finger rays, forward-facing nostrils, a full set of ear hillocks, a straightening trunk; the NHS grape on the way to next week's raspberry, inside a womb the size of a lemon. Myth one, lifting: 64% of 1,084 Americans believe it causes miscarriage and 76% blame stress (Bardos 2015); ACOG puts early loss at 10% of recognised pregnancies, 80% in the first trimester, ~50% chromosomal, with age and prior loss the named risk factors; the uterus is still inside the bony pelvis (Day 53). Thirty pooled studies: lifting >100 kg/day OR 1.32 (0.93–1.87), 1.02 in the better ones (Bonde 2013). The one real signal: 71,500 Danish working women, 2,830 fetal deaths — early miscarriage HR 1.38 at 101–200 kg/day, 2.02 above 1,000 kg/day, 2.74 (1.42–5.26) for >10 lifts of >20 kg a day, no stillbirth signal, and only 52 of 1,266 early losses recorded prospectively (Juhl 2013). Strain in the implantation window RR 2.5 (Hjollund 2000) — a window that closed on Day 23. Exercise: Madsen's HR 3.7 for >7 h/week, recalled after the loss, against Davenport's 46 studies and 266,778 women, miscarriage OR 0.88 (0.63–1.21). NIOSH-derived provisional occupational limits: 36 lb occasional / 18 lb repetitive before 20 weeks, 26 / 13 after (MacDonald & Waters 2013). Verdict: wrong for every lift at home; half right for an eight-hour lifting job, which is an employer conversation. Myth two, the cord: no guideline addresses it because no one has needed to; cord length is set by fetal movement pulling on it (Miller 1981), term length 50–60 cm; a nuchal cord is present in 12% at 24–26 weeks and 37% at term, wrapping and unwrapping (Clapp 2003), 33.7% of 11,748 term deliveries with no change in delivery or Apgar (Schäffer 2005), 14.7% of 166,318 deliveries with perinatal mortality 11 vs 16 per 1,000 (Sheiner 2006), 6.6% tight and 21.6% loose in 219,337 births with no clinically significant harm (Henry 2013), stillbirth OR 1.11 (0.62–1.98) across 145 studies (Hayes 2020), and entanglement in 20.7% of 856,300 Norwegian births driven by long cords, themselves predicted by maternal height, parity, BMI and diabetes (Linde 2018). The one true hazard of arms overhead is a first-trimester dizzy spell on a stepladder (Days 30, 44). Myth three, eating for two: the estimated energy requirement is +0 kcal/day in the first trimester, +340 in the second, +452 in the third (IOM DRI), and the measured cost is ~90, 290 and 470 kcal/day, ~77,000 kcal in total (Butte & King 2005); NICE: no need to eat for two, energy needs unchanged in the first six months, ~200 kcal/day in the last three; NHS: 'there's no need to eat for 2', even with twins. The embryo eats through the yolk sac and uterine glands (Day 51); what the trimester needs is folate, iodine, iron and fish, not calories. IOM bands (11.5–16 kg for normal BMI; 0.5–2 kg in the first trimester); 47.5% of 3.1 million US women gained above the band, 20.4% below (Deputy 2015); 1.3 million women — above-band gain: LGA OR 1.85, macrosomia 1.95, caesarean 1.30; below-band: SGA 1.53, preterm 1.70 (Goldstein 2017); 47.5% of 7,985 first-time mothers already over the band by 15–18 weeks with more gestational diabetes (Carreno 2012). The other edge: dieting not recommended (NICE); nausea weight loss is ordinary (Day 37); early-gestation famine tripled coronary disease without lowering birth weight (Roseboom 2000). The three dinner-table sentences, the baseline weigh-in, and question twelve for the lifting job.
action: Ten minutes tonight, two things. One: on the Myths page of the pregnancy file, write this week's three answers in your own words, short enough for a family dinner — 'lifting's fine; it's an eight-hour-a-day lifting job that's the question'; 'the cord's length is the baby's doing, and a third of babies are born with it round their neck and do fine'; 'zero extra calories till Day 91, a sandwich a day after'. Two: weigh her once this week, same scale, in the morning, and write the number and date in the pregnancy file as the baseline the weight-gain band is measured from; then the scale goes under the bed until the first visit. If her job involves lifting more than 20 kg more than ten times a shift, add question twelve to the Day 40 sheet: lifting at work, and what the note to the employer should say.
